tool.name: Python
tool.tagline: Readable general-purpose language for scripting, data, automation and the web
tool.description: Python is a high-level, dynamically typed language known for readable syntax and a huge standard library and package ecosystem. It is used for automation, web back ends, data analysis, machine learning, scientific computing and teaching. Learning it pays off quickly: small scripts are easy, and the same language scales to large production systems.

glossary.def: In Python, a group of lines indented the same amount under a line ending in a colon (like `if x:` or `def f():`). The lines run together, as one unit.
A text in quotes on the first line inside a function, class or module, describing what it does. Python keeps it, and help() and code editors show it.
A function's name together with its list of parameters (and, if given, their types and its result type): what a caller is allowed to pass in.
A parameter that callers must pass by writing its name, like timeout=5; in Python, the parameters after a lone * or after *args.
A parameter that callers must pass by position, without its name; in Python, the parameters before a / in the definition.
A function that can be treated like any other value: stored in a variable, passed to another function, or returned from one.
Python's one-line way to build a list, dict or set from other items, like [n * n for n in nums if n > 0].
A comprehension in round brackets, like (n * n for n in nums). It hands out its values one at a time when asked instead of building a whole list.
Assigning the items of a tuple or list to several names at once, as in x, y = point.
A method whose name starts and ends with two underscores, like __init__ or __len__. Python calls it for you at certain moments, such as len(x) calling x.__len__().
A variable defined directly in a class body rather than on one object; it is shared by every instance of the class.
The fixed order in which Python searches a class and its parent classes for a method or attribute; super() follows it.
Judging an object by what it can do (which methods it has) rather than what class it is: if it walks and quacks like a duck, treat it as a duck.
A Python class marked with @dataclass, which writes the setup, display and equality methods for you from a list of typed fields.
A tuple whose positions also have names, so you can write p.x instead of p[0]; it still can't be changed.
An object used with Python's with statement that runs a setup step at the start and a clean-up step at the end, even if an error happens; an open file is one.
An object stored on a class that controls what happens when an attribute of that name is read or set, using __get__ and __set__ methods. Properties and methods work this way.
A method taken from an object, with that object already attached as self, so calling it needs only the remaining arguments.
The class of a class: it controls how a class is created and behaves. In Python the default is type.
The standard Python interpreter, written in C, that you get from python.org. Other implementations, like PyPy, exist.
Python Enhancement Proposal: a numbered public document describing a change to Python or a convention, such as PEP 8, the style guide.
The Python Package Index: the public website where Python packages are published and from which pip downloads them.
Python's standard tool for installing packages, usually from PyPI: python -m pip install requests.
The standard settings file for a Python project: its name, version, dependencies, how to build it, and settings for tools like pytest.
The tool named in pyproject.toml that turns a project's source files into installable files (wheels and sdists), such as hatchling or setuptools.
A ready-to-install Python package file (ending in .whl); installing it just copies files, with no build step.
A source distribution: a .tar.gz archive of a Python project's source files, which must be built before installing.
A Python project layout that puts the package's code in a src/ folder, so tests run against the installed package rather than loose files.
Installing your own project with pip install -e . so the environment points at your source folder; edits take effect without reinstalling.
The most widely used Python test runner: tests are plain functions using assert, and it reports exactly which values differed.
A function defined with async def. Calling it gives a coroutine object that only runs when awaited or turned into a task.
Python's built-in way to turn an object into bytes and back, for example to send it to another process. Only load pickles you trust.
A module written in C (or a similar compiled language) that Python can import like any other, usually for speed. NumPy is built on them.
An optional build of Python 3.13+ (python3.13t) without the GIL, so several threads can run Python code on different cores at once.
A reference that lets you reach an object without keeping it alive; once nothing else refers to it, the object is freed and the weak reference goes empty.
In CPython 3.12+, an object such as None or a small int whose reference count is fixed and never updated, so it is never freed.
Part of Python's import machinery that looks for a requested module (for example on disk) and says how to load it.
Part of Python's import machinery that actually runs a found module's code to create the module object.
A small description Python's import machinery produces for a module: its name, where it was found, and which loader will load it.
A Python package folder without an __init__.py file; its parts can be spread over several folders.
CPython's interpreter since 3.11, which replaces often-run bytecode instructions with versions tuned for the types it has actually seen.
In Python's match statement, the part after case that describes a shape a value may have, like [x, y] or {"type": "click"}.
In a match statement, a bare name such as case x: that matches any value and stores it in that name.
A new name for an existing type, such as type UserId = int, so long or repeated types are easier to read.
A group of objects the garbage collector checks together. New objects are checked often; objects that survive are moved to older groups checked rarely.

concepts.name: Running Python: REPL and scripts
concepts.summary: Type Python one line at a time in the REPL, or save instructions in a .py file and run them all at once.
concepts.why: Every later lesson asks you to try code yourself, so you need both ways of running it.
concepts.body:
A program is a list of instructions for a computer, written in a **programming language**: a strict, simplified kind of writing that a computer can follow. Python is one of the most popular, because its instructions read almost like short English sentences.

To carry out those instructions you need the Python **interpreter**. It is a program you install (from python.org, or it may already be on your computer) that reads Python text and does what it says, line by line. When people say "run it with Python", they mean this program.

You start it from a **terminal**: a window where you type commands instead of clicking (Terminal on macOS, PowerShell on Windows). Type `python3` (on Windows, `py`) and press Enter.

You are now in the **REPL**, Python's interactive mode. You type one instruction, press Enter, and Python answers straight away: type `2 + 3` and it shows `5`. The name stands for read-eval-print loop: read what you typed, work it out, print the answer, repeat. Type `exit()` to leave.

For anything longer, write the instructions into a text file whose name ends in `.py`, such as `hello.py`. Use a **code editor** for this: a program for writing and saving text files, like VS Code or even Notepad. A file of Python instructions is called a **script**. Run it from the terminal with `python3 hello.py`. Each complete instruction in it is called a **statement**; Python carries out the statements from top to bottom, then stops.

Unlike the REPL, a script doesn't show results on its own. To see something, use `print(...)`: `print("Hello!")` writes Hello! in the terminal. Text inside quotes is shown exactly as written.

Python is strict about how things are written: its **syntax**, the grammar rules of the language. A missing quote or bracket gives a `SyntaxError`, and nothing in the file runs. Two rules to know now:

- Spaces at the start of a line (indentation) mean something to Python. Don't indent lines at random; later lessons show when to indent, always by four spaces.
- A `#` starts a comment: everything after it on that line is a note for humans, and Python skips it.

Check which version you have with `python3 --version`; this course uses Python 3.13.
concepts.code:
# hello.py  -- run it from the terminal with:  python3 hello.py
print("Hello, world!")     # Hello, world!
print(2 + 3)                # 5
print("2 + 3")              # 2 + 3   (in quotes: shown as written)
2 + 3                       # worked out, but nothing is shown
# This whole line is a comment, so Python skips it.
print("done")               # done
takeaways: `python3` alone opens the REPL; `python3 hello.py` runs a script
A script runs top to bottom and shows only what you `print`
`#` starts a comment; indentation has meaning, so don't indent at random
pitfalls: Typing `python3 hello.py` inside the REPL. That is a terminal command; leave the REPL with `exit()` first.

quiz.q: A script contains two lines: `2 + 3` and `print("done")`. What appears when you run it?
quiz.explain: A script only shows what you print; the sum is worked out but never shown (the REPL would show it).

quiz.q: What does Python do with the text after a `#` on a line?
options: Treats it as a command for the terminal
Ignores it: it's a comment for humans
quiz.explain: `#` starts a comment, which Python skips; it exists only to explain the code to people.

concepts.name: Variables and built-in types
concepts.summary: Give values names with variables, and meet the basic kinds of value: whole numbers, decimals, text, True/False and None.
concepts.why: Every program has to remember things, and the kind of a value decides what you can do with it.
concepts.body:
Programs need to remember things: a price, someone's name, a running total. A **variable** is a name that refers to a value, like a sticky label you put on it. You create one with `=`, as in `price = 3`.

Read `=` as "now refers to", not "equals". After `price = 3`, writing `price` anywhere means 3. Assign again, `price = 4`, and the label now sits on the new value.

Every value has a **data type**: the kind of thing it is, which decides what you can do with it. The ones you'll use from day one:

- `int`: an **integer**, a whole number such as `3`, `-12` or `1000000`
- `float`: a **floating-point number**, a number with a decimal point such as `2.5`
- `str`: a **string**, a piece of text in quotes, `"hello"` or `'hello'`
- `bool`: a **boolean**, one of the two values `True` or `False`
- `None`: a special value meaning "nothing here yet"

`print`, `type` and `int` are **functions**: named actions built into Python. You use one by writing its name followed by parentheses, with the value it should work on inside. `type(price)` tells you the type of the value `price` refers to.

A name has no fixed type; only the value does. `price = "three"` is allowed, and now `price` refers to text. Languages that work like this are called **dynamically typed**. It's convenient, but it also means a mistake can quietly put the wrong kind of value in a name.

Python won't guess when you mix kinds that don't fit. `"3" + 4` is an error (`TypeError`), because Python can't tell whether you meant text or a sum. You convert yourself, which is called **type conversion**: `int("42")` turns text into the number 42, `str(42)` turns the number into the text `"42"`.

Names may use letters, digits and underscores, but can't start with a digit. They are **case-sensitive**: `Price` and `price` are two different names. Python style is lower case with underscores, like `unit_price`.
concepts.code:
price = 3
print(price)              # 3
print(type(price))        # <class 'int'>

price = "three"           # same name, now refers to text
print(type(price))        # <class 'str'>

print(type(2.5), type(True))   # <class 'float'> <class 'bool'>
# print(a, b) shows both values, separated by a space

print(int("42") + 1)      # 43   (text converted to a number first)
print(str(42) + "!")      # 42!  (number converted to text first)

answer = None
print(answer)             # None
takeaways: `name = value` makes a name refer to a value; assigning again points it at a new value
Basic types: `int`, `float`, `str`, `bool` and `None`
Python won't mix text and numbers for you; convert with `int()`, `float()` or `str()`
pitfalls: Naming a variable `str`, `int` or `print`, which hides Python's built-in function of that name.

quiz.q: What happens when Python runs `"3" + 4`?
quiz.explain: Python won't mix text and a number on its own; convert one side first, such as `int("3") + 4`.

quiz.q: After `x = 5` and then `x = "five"`, what does `type(x)` report?
options: An error, because x was already an int
quiz.explain: The name has no fixed type; it now refers to a string, so its type is `str`.

concepts.name: Numbers and arithmetic
concepts.summary: Do arithmetic with Python's operators, including whole-number division, remainders and powers, and know why decimals are approximate.
concepts.why: Calculations are everywhere, and division and decimal results are where beginners most often get surprised.
concepts.body:
Python works as a calculator. The signs that do the work, such as `+` and `*`, are called **operators**:

- `+`, `-` and `*` add, subtract and multiply
- `/` divides and always gives a float: `7 / 2` is `3.5`, and `4 / 2` is `2.0`
- `//` is **integer division**: divide, then round down to a whole number, so `7 // 2` is `3`
- `%` gives the remainder: `7 % 2` is `1`, handy for "is this number even?"
- `**` raises to a power: `2 ** 3` is `8`

If either number is a float, the result is a float: `2 + 1.0` is `3.0`. Brackets work as in school maths, so `(2 + 3) * 4` is `20`.

"Round down" means toward the smaller number, even for negatives: `-7 // 2` is `-4`, not `-3`, because -4 is smaller than -3.5.

Integers can be as large as you like: `2 ** 200` just works. Write long numbers with underscores for readability, `1_000_000`; Python ignores them.

To change a variable based on its own value, write `total = total + 5`, or the shortcut `total += 5`. The same shortcut exists for the other operators, such as `n *= 2`.

Floats are approximate. Computers store numbers in **binary**, using only the digits 0 and 1, and in binary most decimals can't be written exactly, just as 1/3 can't be written exactly as 0.333… So `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is `False` (`==` asks "are these equal?"). For money, Python's `decimal` toolbox does exact decimal sums.

Useful built-in functions: `abs()`, `min()`, `max()` and `round()`. Note that `round(2.5)` gives `2`: Python rounds an exact half to the nearest even number, which avoids always pushing totals upward.

More maths lives in Python's `math` toolbox. Write `import math` at the top of a script, and then `math.sqrt(16)` (square root) and `math.pi` work. The imports lesson explains `import` properly.
concepts.code:
import math                      # load Python's maths toolbox

print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2)      # 3.5 3 1
print(-7 // 2)                   # -4  (rounds down, to the smaller number)
print(2 ** 100)                  # 1267650600228229401496703205376

total = 10
total += 5
print(total)                     # 15

print(0.1 + 0.2)                 # 0.30000000000000004
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)          # False
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))   # True  ("close enough?")

print(round(2.5), round(3.5))    # 2 4
print(math.sqrt(16), 1_000_000 * 3)   # 4.0 3000000
takeaways: `/` always gives a float; `//` divides and rounds down; `%` gives the remainder
Integers never get too big; floats are close approximations
Don't compare floats with `==`; use `math.isclose()`
pitfalls: Checking `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` and being surprised by `False`.
Expecting `round(2.5)` to be 3; Python rounds exact halves to the even number.

quiz.q: What does `-7 // 2` evaluate to?
quiz.explain: `//` rounds down to the smaller whole number, and the smaller one next to -3.5 is -4.

quiz.q: Which expression is a float?
quiz.explain: Division with `/` always gives a float, here 4.0; the others stay whole numbers when both sides are.

concepts.name: Strings and f-strings
concepts.summary: Work with text: pick out characters, change case, split and join, and build messages with f-strings.
concepts.why: Almost every program reads, builds or prints text, and f-strings are the modern way to fill values into it.
concepts.body:
A string is text in quotes. Single and double quotes mean the same thing: `'hi'` and `"hi"` are equal. Triple quotes (`"""..."""`) let text run over several lines. Strings can hold any characters, including accents and emoji.

Some characters are typed with a backslash, called an **escape sequence**: `\n` starts a new line and `\t` inserts a tab. The line break that `\n` produces is called a **newline**.

Every character has a position number, its **index**, counted from 0. In `s = "Python"`, `s[0]` is `"P"` and `s[1]` is `"y"`. Negative numbers count from the end: `s[-1]` is `"n"`. `len(s)` gives the number of characters, 6.

`+` joins strings end to end, which is called **concatenation**: `"ab" + "cd"` is `"abcd"`. `*` repeats: `"ha" * 3` is `"hahaha"`. `"th" in "Python"` checks whether one piece of text appears inside another, giving `True`.

Strings come with built-in actions you call with a dot after the string. These are called **methods**: a method is a function that belongs to a particular kind of value.

- `s.upper()`, `s.lower()` change case; `s.strip()` removes spaces and newlines from both ends (all such blank characters are called **whitespace**)
- `s.replace("old", "new")`, `s.startswith("Py")`
- `s.split(",")` cuts text into pieces and gives a list of them (lists are a later lesson); `", ".join(pieces)` glues them back together

A string can never be changed in place; it is **immutable**. So `s.upper()` doesn't change `s`. It gives back a new string, which you keep with `s = s.upper()`.

An **f-string** fills values into text: put `f` before the quotes and variables in curly braces, `f"Hi {name}"`. After a colon you can say how to display the value:

- `{price:.2f}` two decimal places, `{n:,}` commas in big numbers, `{ratio:.1%}` as a percentage
- `{name:>10}` right-aligned in 10 characters (`<` left, `^` centre)
- `{total=}` shows `total=` and then the value, handy while hunting mistakes
concepts.code:
name = "Ada Lovelace"
print(name[0], name[-1], len(name))   # A e 12
print(name.upper())                   # ADA LOVELACE
print(name.split())                   # ['Ada', 'Lovelace']
print("-".join(["2026", "10", "16"]))  # 2026-10-16
print("love" in name.lower())         # True

price = 4.5
qty = 1234
print(f"{qty:,} items at ${price:.2f}")   # 1,234 items at $4.50
print(f"{0.256:.1%}")                     # 25.6%

total = price * 3
print(f"{total=}")                  # total=13.5
print("line one\nline two")           # prints on two lines
takeaways: Index characters from 0, or from the end with -1
Strings are immutable: methods like `upper()` give back a new string
f-strings fill in values: `f"{price:.2f}"`, `f"{n:,}"`
pitfalls: Calling `s.upper()` and expecting `s` itself to change.
Forgetting the `f` before the quotes, so `{name}` is printed literally.

quiz.q: What does `f"{7/3:.2f}"` produce?
quiz.explain: The `.2f` spec formats the float with exactly two digits after the decimal point.

quiz.q: After `s = "hi"; s.upper()`, what is `s`?
quiz.explain: Strings are immutable; `upper()` gave back a new string, which was thrown away because nothing kept it.

concepts.name: Booleans, comparisons and if
concepts.summary: Make decisions with if, elif and else, comparisons like < and ==, and the words and, or, not.
concepts.why: Making choices is the step from a calculator to a program: do this when that is true.
concepts.body:
Programs often have to choose: if the cart is empty, show a message; otherwise, show the total. Python decides with comparisons, which give a boolean, `True` or `False`.

- `==` equal, `!=` not equal (a single `=` assigns; it never compares)
- `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` smaller, at most, bigger, at least
- They can be chained: `0 <= x < 10` means x is from 0 up to, but not including, 10

Combine checks with the words `and` (both must be true), `or` (at least one) and `not` (flips True and False).

An `if` line ends with a colon, and the lines under it are indented by four spaces. Those indented lines form a **block**: a group of lines that belong together. This block runs only when the check is true. `elif` ("else if") adds another check, and `else` catches everything left. Only the first block whose check is true runs. Code like this, which runs only under a condition, is called a **conditional**.

Python also treats other values as true or false. Values that count as false are called **falsy**: `False`, `None`, `0`, `0.0`, the empty string `""`, and empty collections such as the empty list `[]` you'll meet next. Everything else is **truthy**. So `if name:` means "if name isn't empty".

`and` and `or` stop as soon as the answer is known; this is called **short-circuit evaluation**. `or` also gives back the value that decided it, not just True or False. So `name = typed or "anonymous"` keeps what was typed, unless it was empty, in which case it uses "anonymous".

For a quick choice between two values, write it in one line: `label = "even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd"`.

To check for `None`, write `x is None`. `is` asks "is this the very same thing?", while `==` asks "are these equal?". Use `==` everywhere else.
concepts.code:
temp = 21
if temp < 0:
    print("freezing")
elif temp < 18:
    print("cold")
elif temp <= 25:
    print("pleasant")            # this branch runs
else:
    print("hot")

print(0 <= 5 < 10)                 # True
print(temp > 0 and temp < 10)      # False

typed = ""
if not typed:
    print("nothing typed")         # nothing typed
name = typed or "anonymous"
print(name)                        # anonymous

n = 7
print("even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd")   # odd
takeaways: `if` / `elif` / `else`: only the first block whose check is true runs
`0`, `""`, `None` and empty collections count as false
`==` compares values; use `is` only for `x is None`
pitfalls: Writing `=` (assign) where you meant `==` (compare).
Using `or` for defaults when 0 or "" is a real answer, since they count as false too.

quiz.q: What does `"" or "default"` give?
quiz.explain: `or` gives back the first truthy value; the empty string counts as false, so the result is "default".

quiz.q:
With `x = 15`, which line prints?
`if x > 10: print("A")` / `elif x > 5: print("B")` / `else: print("C")`
quiz.explain: Only the first branch whose check is true runs; `x > 10` is already true, so only A prints.

concepts.name: Lists
concepts.summary: Keep many values in order in one list: read them by position, add, remove and sort.
concepts.why: Most programs handle collections of things (names, prices, files), and the list is Python's everyday way to hold them.
concepts.body:
A **list** holds several values in order, written in square brackets with commas between: `nums = [3, 1, 4]`, or `names = ["Ana", "Ben"]`. Think of a numbered shopping list.

Positions work like string indexes, starting at 0: `nums[0]` is the first item and `nums[-1]` the last. Asking for a position that doesn't exist gives an `IndexError`. `len(nums)` counts the items, and `4 in nums` checks whether a value is there.

Unlike strings, lists can be changed after they're made: they are **mutable**. You can replace an item, `nums[0] = 10`, or use list methods:

- `append(x)` adds `x` to the end; `extend([5, 9])` adds every item of another list
- `insert(i, x)` puts `x` before position `i`
- `pop()` removes the last item and gives it back; `remove(x)` deletes the first item equal to `x`
- `sort()` puts the list in order; `reverse()` flips it

These methods change the list itself and give back `None` (nothing). So `nums = nums.sort()` is a mistake: the list gets sorted, and then `nums` is set to `None`.

If you want a sorted copy and to keep the original as it was, use the built-in function `sorted(nums)`. Both ways accept `reverse=True`. You can also sort by something other than the value itself: `sorted(words, key=len)` sorts words by their length.

`+` joins two lists into a new one, and `[0] * 5` makes `[0, 0, 0, 0, 0]`.

Adding and removing at the end of a list is quick. Inserting or removing at the front, and checking `x in nums`, get slow when a list holds many thousands of items, because Python has to shift or check every item one by one.
concepts.code:
nums = [3, 1, 4]
nums.append(1)
nums.extend([5, 9])
print(nums)            # [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9]
print(nums[0], nums[-1], len(nums))   # 3 9 6

last = nums.pop()
print(last, nums)      # 9 [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]

print(sorted(nums))    # [1, 1, 3, 4, 5]  (new list)
print(nums)            # [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]  (unchanged)
nums.sort(reverse=True)
print(nums)            # [5, 4, 3, 1, 1]

words = ["kiwi", "fig", "banana"]
print(sorted(words, key=len))   # ['fig', 'kiwi', 'banana']
print(nums.sort())     # None  -- sort() changes the list, gives back nothing
takeaways: Lists are ordered and mutable; positions start at 0, and -1 is the last item
`nums.sort()` changes the list and gives back None; `sorted(nums)` gives a new sorted list
Add and remove at the end; working at the front gets slow on very long lists
pitfalls: Writing `nums = nums.sort()`, which sets `nums` to None.

quiz.q: What is `x` after `x = [2, 1]; y = x.append(3)`?
quiz.explain: `append` changes `x` itself (and gives back None, which is what `y` gets).

concepts.name: for and while loops
concepts.summary: Repeat work with for (once per item) and while (as long as a check is true), plus range, enumerate, zip, break and continue.
concepts.why: Loops let a few lines of code handle every item in a list, every line in a file, or every try at an answer.
concepts.body:
To print every name in a list you could write one `print` per name, but that breaks as soon as the list changes. A **loop** repeats a block of code for you. Each pass through it is called an **iteration**.

A `for` loop runs its block once for each item: `for name in names:` sets `name` to the first item, runs the indented block, then goes on to the next item. It works on anything made of items: a list, a string (one character at a time), and other collections you'll meet later.

To repeat a fixed number of times use `range`: `range(5)` gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. `range(2, 10, 2)` gives 2, 4, 6, 8 (start, stop, step). The stop number is never included.

Helpers that make loops clearer:

- `enumerate(items, start=1)` gives pairs of a counter and an item; writing two names, `for i, name in ...`, catches both parts of each pair
- `zip(names, scores)` walks two lists side by side, stopping at the end of the shorter one
- `reversed(items)` and `sorted(items)` loop backwards or in order

A `while` loop repeats as long as its check is true. Use it when you don't know in advance how many passes you need, such as asking again until the answer is valid. Make sure something inside changes the check, or the loop never ends.

Inside any loop, `break` leaves the loop at once and `continue` skips straight to the next pass. A loop can also end with an `else` block, which runs only if the loop finished without a `break`. That's handy for searches: "not found".

Don't add or remove items from a list while a `for` loop is going through it; the loop gets confused and skips items. Build a new list instead.
takeaways: `for x in items` runs the block once per item; no counting needed
`range(start, stop, step)` never includes `stop`
Use `enumerate` for a counter and `zip` to walk two lists together
pitfalls: Adding or removing items from a list while looping over it.
A `while` loop whose check never becomes false, so it runs forever (press Ctrl-C to stop it).

quiz.q: What does `list(range(1, 8, 3))` produce?
quiz.explain: Start at 1, step by 3, stop before 8: 1, 4, 7.

quiz.q: When does the `else` block of a `for` loop run?
options: When the loop ends without a `break`
Only if the loop body never ran
When something goes wrong in the loop
After every pass through the loop
quiz.explain: The `else` block runs when the loop finishes normally; a `break` skips it.

concepts.name: Names, references and mutability
concepts.summary: Assigning never copies: two names can share one list, and changing it through one name shows through the other.
concepts.why: This explains one of the most common beginner surprises: a list that changes when you didn't touch it.
concepts.body:
Python keeps every value (a number, a string, a list) as an **object**: one thing stored in the computer's **memory** (where a running program keeps its data), with a type and a value. A variable is a label stuck on an object. Assigning never copies the object; it only sticks on another label.

So after `b = a`, both names refer to the **same** list. A name that refers to an object this way is often called a **reference** to it. Whether sharing matters depends on whether the object can change.

- Immutable objects (`int`, `float`, `str`, `bool`, tuples) never change. Anything that seems to change them actually makes a new object, so sharing them is harmless.
- Mutable objects (lists, and the dictionaries and sets you'll meet soon) can be changed in place. That change is visible through every name that refers to them.

Compare two ways of adding to `b` after `b = a`. `b.append(4)` changes the shared list, so `a` sees the 4 too. `b = b + [4]` builds a new list and puts only the label `b` on it, so `a` is left alone.

`a is b` asks "are these two names on the very same object?", while `a == b` asks "do they hold equal values?". Two separate lists can be equal without being the same list.

When you want an independent copy, ask for one: `items.copy()` or `list(items)` makes a new list. That copy is **shallow**: if the list holds other lists, the copy holds those same inner lists. For a list of lists, `copy.deepcopy(items)` (from Python's `copy` toolbox) copies the inner lists too, all the way down.

A classic mistake is making a grid with `[[0] * 3] * 3`. The outer `* 3` repeats a label to one inner list three times, so changing `grid[0][0]` (the first number in the first row) changes the first number of every row. Build each inner list separately in a loop instead, as the example shows.
concepts.code:
import copy                  # Python's copying toolbox

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a                        # second label on the same list
b.append(4)
print(a, a is b)             # [1, 2, 3, 4] True

c = a.copy()                 # a new, separate list
c.append(5)
print(a, c)                  # [1, 2, 3, 4] [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(a == [1, 2, 3, 4], a is [1, 2, 3, 4])   # True False

bad = [[0] * 2] * 2          # one inner list, labelled twice
bad[0][0] = 9
print(bad)                   # [[9, 0], [9, 0]]

good = []
for _ in range(2):           # _ is a name for "I don't need this value"
    good.append([0] * 2)     # a fresh inner list each time
good[0][0] = 9
print(good)                  # [[9, 0], [0, 0]]

nested = [["a"]]
deep = copy.deepcopy(nested)
deep[0].append("b")
print(nested)                # [['a']]
takeaways: Assigning sticks another label on the same object; it never copies
Changing a mutable object shows through every name that refers to it
`.copy()` makes a shallow copy; `copy.deepcopy()` copies lists inside lists too
pitfalls: Making a grid with `[[0] * n] * m`, so every row is the same list.

quiz.q: After `x = [1]; y = x; y = y + [2]`, what is `x`?
quiz.explain: `y + [2]` builds a new list and puts only the label `y` on it; the list `x` refers to is untouched.

quiz.q: After `x = [1]; y = x; y += [2]`, what is `x`?
quiz.explain: For lists, `+=` adds to the existing list in place, so the shared list changes and `x` sees it.

concepts.name: Tuples and unpacking
concepts.summary: Tuples are fixed, unchangeable groups of values; unpacking pulls their parts into separate names in one line.
concepts.why: Tuples hold small fixed groups of values, like a point or a (name, age) pair, and unpacking makes them easy to use.
concepts.body:
A **tuple** is like a list that can never change. It's written with round brackets: `point = (3, 4)`. Once made, you can't add, remove or replace its items: it's immutable.

It's actually the comma that makes a tuple, not the brackets: `t = 1, 2` is a tuple too. That's why a tuple with one item needs a trailing comma, `(5,)`, while `(5)` is just the number 5 in brackets. `()` is an empty tuple.

You read tuples like lists: `point[0]` is 3, `len(point)` is 2, and you can loop over them. Use a tuple when each position has a fixed meaning: a point (x, y), a colour as red, green and blue amounts `(255, 128, 0)`, or a `(name, age)` pair. Use a list when you have any number of similar items.

Unpacking (or **tuple unpacking**) puts the items of a tuple, or a list, into several names at once:

- `x, y = point` sets `x` to 3 and `y` to 4
- `first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]` gives `first` 1 and puts the leftovers in a list, `rest == [2, 3, 4]`
- `for name, age in people:` unpacks each pair as the loop goes
- `a, b = b, a` swaps two variables in one line

Because they can't change, tuples can be used where Python needs a value that stays put, such as the keys of a dictionary (next lesson). Later you'll also see functions give back several results at once as a tuple.

When a tuple has many items, code like `row[3]` stops saying what it means. Later lessons show ways to give each position a name.

A tuple only stops you swapping its items. If one item is a list, that list itself can still be changed.
concepts.code:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x, y)               # 3 4

single = (5,)
print(type(single), type((5)))   # <class 'tuple'> <class 'int'>

values = [7, 2, 9]
lo, hi = min(values), max(values)   # build a tuple, unpack it
print(lo, hi)             # 2 9

first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(first, rest)        # 1 [2, 3, 4]

a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a               # swap
print(a, b)               # 2 1

people = [("Ana", 31), ("Ben", 27)]
for name, age in people:
    print(f"{name} is {age}")   # Ana is 31 / Ben is 27
takeaways: The comma makes a tuple; `(x,)` is a one-item tuple
Tuples can't be changed after they're made
Unpacking (`x, y = point`, `first, *rest = items`) splits values into names
pitfalls: Writing `(5)` and expecting a tuple.

quiz.q: What is `type(("a"))`?
quiz.explain: Brackets alone just group; without a trailing comma it's the string 'a', so the type is str.

concepts.name: Dictionaries
concepts.summary: Look values up by a key, like words in a dictionary; add, update and loop over them, and read safely with get().
concepts.why: Whenever you look things up by name (prices by product, counts by word, settings by key) you use a dictionary.
concepts.body:
A list finds things by position. Often you want to find them by name instead: the price of "tea", the age of "ana". A **dictionary** (`dict`) stores pairs of a **key** and a value, like words and their meanings: `ages = {"ana": 31, "ben": 27}`. Each key-value pair is written `key: value`.

You look up with the key in square brackets: `ages["ana"]` is 31. Lookups stay fast however big the dict grows, because Python turns each key into a number, its **hash**, that tells it where to look, instead of checking every entry. That only works if a key never changes, so keys must be immutable: strings, numbers or tuples. A list can't be a key.

Asking for a missing key with `d[key]` stops the program with a `KeyError`. When a key might be missing:

- `d.get(key)` gives `None` if it's absent, and `d.get(key, 0)` gives 0 instead
- `key in d` checks whether the key exists (it checks keys, not values)

To add or change, assign: `d[key] = value` adds the key if it's new and replaces the value if not. `del d[key]` removes a key. `d1 | d2` makes a new dict with both, where `d2` wins if a key is in both.

A dict keeps keys in the order you added them. A `for` loop over a dict gives its keys. For keys and values together, loop over `d.items()`, which gives `(key, value)` pairs to unpack: `for name, age in ages.items():`. `d.keys()` and `d.values()` give just one side.

Counting is a classic dict job: `counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1` starts each new word at 0 and adds 1.

Don't add or remove keys while looping over the same dict; Python stops with an error. Loop over `list(d)`, a copy of the keys, if you need to.
takeaways: A dict maps keys to values; keys must be immutable, like strings, numbers or tuples
Use `.get()` or `in` when a key may be missing
Loop with `for k, v in d.items()`; dicts keep the order keys were added
pitfalls: Reading `d[key]` for a key that might not exist and getting `KeyError`.

quiz.q: Which of these can be a dict key?
quiz.explain: A tuple of immutable values can be a key; lists, dicts and sets can change, so they can't be keys.

quiz.q: What does `for x in {"a": 1, "b": 2}:` iterate over?
options: Nothing; you can't loop over a dict
quiz.explain: Looping over a dict gives its keys; use `.items()` for pairs.

concepts.name: Sets
concepts.summary: Sets hold each value once, check "is x in here?" instantly, and combine groups with union and intersection.
concepts.why: Sets remove duplicates and answer "have I seen this?" fast, even with millions of items.
concepts.body:
A **set** is a collection where each value appears only once, and there is no order: `tags = {"python", "web"}`. Adding a value that's already there does nothing.

Sets work like the keys of a dict: Python uses each value's hash to find it. So `x in s` is fast even for a huge set, while on a long list it has to check item by item. Use a set whenever a loop asks "have I seen this one before?". Like dict keys, set items must be immutable.

Watch out: `{}` is an empty **dict**, not a set. An empty set is written `set()`.

`set(items)` removes duplicates from a list: `set([1, 2, 2, 3])` is `{1, 2, 3}`. A set has no order, so if you need to keep the original order while removing duplicates, use `list(dict.fromkeys(items))` instead, because dicts remember order.

Change a set with `add(x)`, `discard(x)` (no error if `x` isn't there) and `remove(x)` (a `KeyError` if it isn't).

Sets can be combined like in school maths, with operators:

- `a | b` union: everything in either set
- `a & b` intersection: only what's in both
- `a - b` difference: what's in `a` but not in `b`
- `a <= b` asks whether every item of `a` is also in `b`

A `frozenset` is a set that can't change, so unlike a normal set it can be a dict key or an item in another set.

When you print or loop over a set, the order is unpredictable and can even differ from one run of the program to the next. Use `sorted(s)` when you need a steady order.
takeaways: Sets keep each value once and check membership fast
`{}` is an empty dict; write `set()` for an empty set
`|`, `&` and `-` give union, intersection and difference
pitfalls: Expecting a set to keep items in the order you added them.

quiz.q: What does `len({1, 2} | {2, 3})` return?
quiz.explain: The union is {1, 2, 3}; the shared 2 appears only once.

concepts.name: Defining functions
concepts.summary: Write your own functions with def: give them inputs (parameters), get a result back with return, and set default values.
concepts.why: Functions let you name a piece of work and reuse it, instead of copying the same lines all over a program.
concepts.body:
You've used Python's functions, like `len()` and `print()`. You can write your own with `def`: a name, the inputs in brackets, a colon, and an indented block of code. That block runs each time someone **calls** the function by writing its name with brackets.

The names in the brackets of `def area(width, height):` are **parameters**: placeholders for the inputs. The actual values given in a call, like `area(3, 4)`, are **arguments**. They're matched up in order, or by name: `area(width=3, height=4)`. Passing by name is called a **keyword argument**, and it makes calls easier to read.

`return` hands a result back to whoever called the function and ends it. That result is the **return value**. A function that never reaches a `return` gives back `None`. To give back several results, return a tuple: `return lo, hi`, then unpack it with `lo, hi = min_max(values)`.

A parameter can have a **default value**, used when the caller leaves it out: `def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):`. Parameters with defaults go after those without.

An argument is not copied: the parameter is just another name for the caller's object. So a function that appends to a list it was given changes the caller's list too.

That leads to a famous surprise. A default value is created once, when Python reads the `def`, not on each call. So `def add(item, bucket=[]):` shares one list between all calls, and it keeps growing. Use `None` as the default and make a fresh list inside: `if bucket is None: bucket = []`.

A string on the first line of the body is the function's **docstring**, its built-in description; `help(area)` shows it.

Variables created inside a function are **local variables**: they exist only while it runs. Names created outside any function are **global variables**; a function can read them, but assigning to the same name inside makes a new local one. Pass values in and return results rather than relying on globals.
concepts.code:
def bmi(weight_kg, height_m, digits=1):
    """Return body-mass index rounded to `digits` places."""
    return round(weight_kg / height_m ** 2, digits)

print(bmi(70, 1.75))                              # 22.9
print(bmi(height_m=1.8, weight_kg=81, digits=2))  # 25.0

def min_max(values):
    return min(values), max(values)   # a tuple
lo, hi = min_max([7, 2, 9])
print(lo, hi)                         # 2 9

def add_tag(tag, tags=None):
    if tags is None:                  # fresh list on every call
        tags = []
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags
print(add_tag("a"), add_tag("b"))     # ['a'] ['b']

def nothing():
    pass                              # pass means "do nothing"
print(nothing())                      # None
takeaways: Parameters name the inputs; arguments are the values passed in a call
A function without `return` gives back None
Default values are created once, so use `None` as the default for lists and dicts
pitfalls: Using `[]` or `{}` as a default value; that one list or dict is shared by every call.

quiz.q: Given `def f(x, acc=[]): acc.append(x); return acc`, what does the second call in `f(1); f(2)` return?
quiz.explain: The default list is created once, when Python reads the `def`, so both calls append to the same list.

quiz.q: What does `def double(n): n * 2` give back when called as `double(4)`?
quiz.explain: It works out `n * 2` but never says `return`, so the function gives back None.

concepts.name: Modules and imports
concepts.summary: Split code across files and use Python's ready-made toolboxes with import and from ... import.
concepts.why: Python ships with a large collection of ready-made code, and real programs are spread over many files.
concepts.body:
Every `.py` file is a **module**: a file of Python code that other files can use. Its name is the file name without `.py`, so `geometry.py` is the module `geometry`. A folder of modules is a **package**.

Python comes with hundreds of modules ready to use, called the **standard library**. Using one is called an **import**:

- `import math`, then `math.sqrt(2)`: the `math.` in front shows where the name comes from
- `from math import sqrt, pi`: bring in just those names, then write `sqrt(2)`
- `import random as rnd`: a shorter nickname for a module

Avoid `from module import *`, which pours in every name at once and hides where each one came from.

The first time a program imports a module, Python runs that file from top to bottom, once, and remembers the result. Later imports of the same module just reuse it.

That's why many scripts end with `if __name__ == "__main__":`. Python sets `__name__` to `"__main__"` only in the file you ran directly. So the code under that line runs when you run the file as a script, but not when another file imports it to use its functions.

Python looks for modules first in the folder of the script you ran, then in the standard library, then among extra packages you've installed. So naming your own file `random.py` hides the real `random` module and causes baffling errors.

A collection of ready-made code for others to use is called a **library**. One made outside Python itself, by other people, is a **third-party library**; you install those separately (see the virtual environments lesson).

A few standard modules you'll use a lot: `math`, `random`, `datetime` (dates and times), `json` and `csv` (reading common data files), `pathlib` (files and folders), `re` (finding text that fits a description, such as "any run of digits") and `collections` (extra kinds of collections).

By convention, imports go at the top of the file: standard library first, then third-party libraries, then your own modules.
concepts.code:
# geometry.py could contain:  def circle_area(r): ...
# and another file could then use:  from geometry import circle_area
import math
import random as rnd
from datetime import date
from collections import Counter

print(math.sqrt(16), math.pi)          # 4.0 3.141592653589793
print(date(2026, 1, 1).isoformat())    # 2026-01-01
print(Counter("banana").most_common(1))  # [('a', 3)]  counts letters
print(rnd.randint(1, 6))               # a random number from 1 to 6

def main():
    print("running as a script")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()                             # skipped when imported
takeaways: Every .py file is a module; `import` lets another file use it
A module's code runs once per program; later imports reuse it
`if __name__ == "__main__":` holds code that should run only as a script
pitfalls: Naming your own file after a standard module, like `random.py` or `json.py`.
Using `from x import *`.

quiz.q: `app.py` runs `import helpers` in two different places. How many times does the code at the top level of helpers.py run?
quiz.explain: The first import runs the module and Python remembers it; the second import reuses it.

quiz.q: `tools.py` ends with `if __name__ == "__main__": main()`. When does `main()` run?
options: Every time any file imports tools
Never; you must call it from the REPL
quiz.explain: Running a file directly sets its `__name__` to "__main__"; when it's imported, `__name__` is the module's name instead.

concepts.name: Errors and try/except
concepts.summary: Read Python's error report, catch the errors you expect with try/except, and raise your own.
concepts.why: Programs meet bad input and missing files; handling errors on purpose keeps them from crashing.
concepts.body:
Mistakes in code are called **bugs**, and some problems only show up while a program runs: text that isn't a number, a file that isn't there. When Python hits one it creates an **exception**, an object describing what went wrong, and "raises" it.

If nothing deals with the exception, the program stops and prints a report called a **traceback**. Read it from the bottom up. The last line names the kind of error and a message, such as `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'`. The lines above list the chain of function calls that led there, newest last, with file names and line numbers.

Common kinds: `ValueError` (right type, bad value), `TypeError` (wrong type), `KeyError` and `IndexError` (missing key or position), `ZeroDivisionError`, `FileNotFoundError` and `NameError` (a name that doesn't exist, often a typo).

A `try` block lets you deal with an exception you expect. This is called **exception handling**:

```python
try:
    n = int(text)
except ValueError:
    n = 0
```

Python runs the `try` block; if a `ValueError` happens there, it jumps to the `except` block instead of stopping.

Put only the line that might fail inside `try`, and catch the **specific** kind you can handle. A bare `except:` that quietly carries on hides real bugs, typos included. Write `except ValueError as e:` to get the exception itself, for example to print its message.

Python style is to try the action and handle the failure, rather than checking everything first. A check can go stale: a file can be deleted between "does it exist?" and opening it.

Raise your own exception with `raise ValueError("age must be positive")` when a function gets input it can't work with. A clear error where the problem starts beats a confusing one later.
takeaways: Read a traceback from the bottom: the kind of error and its message come last
Catch specific exceptions, around only the code that can fail
Raise exceptions with clear messages when input is invalid
pitfalls: Catching everything with a bare `except:` and hiding real bugs.

quiz.q: Which is the best way to convert user text to int with a fallback of 0?
options: `if s.isnumeric(): n = int(s)` and nothing else
quiz.explain: It catches only the expected failure and sets the fallback; a bare except hides other errors, and `int(s) or 0` still stops on bad text.

concepts.name: Reading and writing files
concepts.summary: Open text files with with open(...), read them line by line, and write results back.
concepts.why: Most useful scripts read some file (notes, a spreadsheet export, settings) and write their results to another.
concepts.body:
A file lives on the **disk** (your computer's long-term storage, which keeps files when the power is off) at a **file path**, its address, like `notes.txt` (in the current folder) or `C:\Users\ana\notes.txt`. The built-in `open(path, mode, encoding=...)` gives you a file object to read or write. Always open files in a `with` block, which closes the file for you when the block ends, even if an error happens:

```python
with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    text = f.read()
```

The mode says what you're doing:

- `"r"` read (the default), `"a"` add to the end, `"x"` create a new file, failing if it exists
- `"w"` write: this **empties an existing file first**
- add `"b"` for files that aren't text, like images (`"rb"`, `"wb"`); you then get raw `bytes` instead of strings

Files store **bytes**: small numbers from 0 to 255. An **encoding** is the rule for turning text into bytes and back. Always pass `encoding="utf-8"`, the standard one, called **UTF-8**. Without it, Python uses your computer's own default, which on Windows is often different, so the same script can misread a file on another machine.

`f.read()` gives the whole file as one string. `for line in f:` reads one line per pass instead, which works even for files too big to fit in memory. Each line keeps its newline at the end, so call `line.rstrip("\n")` or `line.strip()`.

`f.write(s)` writes a string and does **not** add a newline for you; `print(..., file=f)` does.

For common data files, use the standard library instead of splitting text yourself. **CSV** files are spreadsheet-like rows of comma-separated values; read them with the `csv` module. **JSON** is a text format for data made of dicts and lists; `json.dump` writes it and `json.load` reads it back.
concepts.code:
import json

with open("todo.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("buy milk\n")
    print("call mum", file=f)       # print adds the newline

with open("todo.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for number, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
        print(number, line.rstrip("\n"))
# 1 buy milk
# 2 call mum

with open("todo.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("water plants\n")

config = {"debug": True, "retries": 3}   # a dict, saved as JSON
with open("config.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(config, f, indent=2)
with open("config.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(json.load(f)["retries"])  # 3
takeaways: Open files in a `with` block so they always close
Pass `encoding="utf-8"` for text files
Loop `for line in f` to read big files one line at a time
pitfalls: Opening an existing file with mode `"w"` and wiping its contents by accident.

quiz.q: You loop `for line in f:` over a text file. What does each `line` usually end with?
quiz.explain: Each line keeps its newline at the end; remove it with `rstrip("\n")` if needed.

concepts.name: Slicing sequences
concepts.summary: Take out, copy, reverse and replace ranges of lists and strings with start:stop:step.
concepts.why: Slicing is the short, standard way to take part of a list or string without writing a loop over indexes.
concepts.body:
A **slice** picks out a range of items from a list, tuple or string, which Python calls sequences (collections whose items have positions). It's written `seq[start:stop:step]`. Like `range`, it includes `start` and stops just before `stop`. Every part is optional:

- `s[:3]` the first three items, `s[3:]` everything from index 3 on
- `s[-2:]` the last two, `s[:-1]` all but the last
- `s[::2]` every second item, `s[::-1]` the whole thing reversed
- `s[:]` a shallow copy of the whole thing

Slices are forgiving. Asking for a position past the end with `s[10]` is an `IndexError`, but slice bounds past the end are simply cut short: `"abc"[1:100]` is `"bc"` and `[][:5]` is `[]`. So "the first n items" is safe even on a short list.

A slice always gives back a **new** list, tuple or string. For a list it's a shallow copy: the new list refers to the same items, but changing the new list (adding, removing, replacing) doesn't change the original.

On a list you can also **assign** to a slice. That replaces the range with the items you give, even a different number of them: `nums[1:3] = [7, 8, 9]`. `del nums[::2]` deletes every second item. When the slice has a step, the replacement must have exactly as many items as the slice.

If the same slice is used in several places, give it a name: `YEAR = slice(0, 4)`, then `date[YEAR]`. The `slice(...)` object is exactly what the colon notation creates behind the scenes.

Every slice copies the items it selects, so on very large data, slicing again and again costs time and memory. Libraries for big numeric data, such as NumPy, offer slices that share data instead of copying.
concepts.code:
letters = "abcdefgh"
print(letters[2:5])      # cde
print(letters[:3], letters[-3:])   # abc fgh
print(letters[::2])      # aceg
print(letters[::-1])     # hgfedcba
print(letters[5:100])    # fgh  (bounds are clipped)

nums = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
copy = nums[:]
copy[0] = 99
print(nums[0])           # 0

nums[1:3] = [7, 8, 9]    # replace 2 items with 3
print(nums)              # [0, 7, 8, 9, 3, 4, 5]
del nums[::2]
print(nums)              # [7, 9, 4]

YEAR = slice(0, 4)
print("2026-10-16"[YEAR])   # 2026
takeaways: `s[start:stop:step]` includes start and stops before stop
Slice bounds past the end are cut short instead of causing an error
`s[::-1]` reverses, `s[:]` makes a shallow copy
pitfalls: Expecting changes to a slice of a list to show up in the original list; a slice is a copy.

quiz.explain: -4 is index 1 (20) and -1 is index 4 (50), which is excluded.

quiz.q: What does `"python"[10:]` return?
quiz.explain: Slice bounds beyond the end are clipped, giving an empty string.

concepts.name: Comprehensions
concepts.summary: Build a new list, dict or set from existing items in one readable line.
concepts.why: Comprehensions replace most "make an empty list, loop, append" code and are everywhere in real Python.
concepts.body:
You often build one list from another: an empty list, a loop, an `append` for each item. A **list comprehension** says the same in one line: `[n * n for n in nums]` means "`n * n`, for each `n` in `nums`". Add `if` at the end to keep only some items: `[n for n in nums if n > 0]`.

The general shape is `[expression for item in iterable if condition]`. Two words in it are worth knowing:

- an **expression** is any piece of code that produces a value, like `n * n`, `name.upper()` or `3`
- an **iterable** is anything a `for` loop can go through: a list, tuple, string, dict, set, `range`, or an open file

The same idea builds other collections:

- dict comprehension: `{name: len(name) for name in names}`
- set comprehension: `{word.lower() for word in words}`

With round brackets you get a **generator expression**, `(x * x for x in nums)`. It doesn't build a list at all; it hands out one value at a time when asked. This is called **lazy evaluation**: work is done only when a value is needed. Pass it straight to a function such as `sum(x * x for x in nums)` to add up a million squares without ever storing them.

The `if` at the end filters. To change some items instead of leaving them out, put the one-line if/else in the expression part: `[x if x > 0 else 0 for x in nums]`.

Several `for` parts nest left to right, like loops inside loops written on one line: `[(r, c) for r in range(3) for c in range(3)]`. One level of nesting reads fine; beyond that, write ordinary loops.

The loop variable inside a comprehension stays inside it: after `[x for x in data]`, there's no new `x` outside.

Use a comprehension to **build** a value. If you only want an action for each item, such as printing it, that action is a **side effect** (something a piece of code does besides producing its value). Write a normal loop for that, and also whenever the comprehension stops fitting comfortably on one or two lines.
concepts.code:
nums = [3, -1, 4, -1, 5, -9]

squares = [n * n for n in nums]
positives = [n for n in nums if n > 0]
clamped = [n if n > 0 else 0 for n in nums]
print(positives)           # [3, 4, 5]
print(clamped)             # [3, 0, 4, 0, 5, 0]

words = ["Apple", "banana", "apple", "Cherry"]
unique = {w.lower() for w in words}
lengths = {w: len(w) for w in words}
print(sorted(unique))      # ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
print(lengths["banana"])   # 6

total = sum(n * n for n in nums)   # generator expression, no list built
print(total)               # 133

grid = [(r, c) for r in range(2) for c in range(3)]
print(grid)   # [(0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 0), (1, 1), (1, 2)]
takeaways: `[expr for x in items if cond]` changes and filters in one expression
`{k: v ...}` builds dicts, `{x ...}` sets, `(x ...)` a lazy generator
Use a plain loop for actions like printing, or anything nested more than once
pitfalls: Putting `else` after the trailing `if` filter; a one-line if/else belongs in the expression part.

quiz.q: What does `[x * 2 for x in range(5) if x % 2]` evaluate to?
quiz.explain: `x % 2` is 1 (truthy) for odd x, so only 1 and 3 are kept; doubling gives [2, 6].

quiz.q: Why is `sum(x*x for x in data)` preferable to `sum([x*x for x in data])` for huge data?
options: It uses several processors at once
It never builds the whole list in memory
It remembers the results for next time
quiz.explain: A generator expression hands out items one at a time, so no big temporary list is created.

concepts.name: *args, **kwargs and parameter kinds
concepts.summary: Accept any number of arguments with *args and **kwargs, force names with keyword-only parameters, and spread lists into calls.
concepts.why: You need these to design clear functions, and to read the definitions of functions other people wrote.
concepts.body:
A function's first line, its name plus its parameter list, is called its **signature**: it tells callers what they may pass. So far each parameter has taken one argument, passed by position or by name. A plain argument matched by its place in the call is a **positional argument**. Python offers a few more kinds of parameter:

- `*args` collects any extra positional arguments into a tuple
- `**kwargs` collects any extra keyword arguments into a dict
- parameters after a lone `*` (or after `*args`) are **keyword-only**: callers must write their names
- parameters before a `/` are **positional-only**: callers can't use their names

The full order is `def f(pos_only, /, normal, *args, kw_only, **kwargs)`.

Keyword-only parameters are a great design tool. `def connect(host, *, timeout=10, retries=3)` forces calls to say `timeout=5`, which keeps them readable. It also lets you reorder or add options later without breaking anyone's code. Positional-only parameters do the reverse: you can rename them freely, since no caller uses the name. Many built-in functions work this way; you can't write `len(obj=x)`.

The same stars work the other way round in a call. `f(*items)` spreads a list or tuple into separate positional arguments, and `f(**options)` spreads a dict into keyword arguments.

Together they allow forwarding: a function that accepts `*args, **kwargs` and passes them straight on to another function, whatever its parameters. That's the basis of decorators, a later lesson.

The names `args` and `kwargs` are only a convention; the stars do the work. Use them when a function truly takes a varying number of things (like `print`) or forwards arguments. Don't use `**kwargs` just to avoid listing parameters. Named parameters document themselves, Python checks them, and code editors can suggest them.
concepts.code:
def log(message, *values, level="INFO", **context):
    extra = " ".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in context.items())
    print(f"[{level}] {message}", *values, extra)

log("started")                         # [INFO] started
log("sum is", 3, 4, level="DEBUG", user="ana")
# [DEBUG] sum is 3 4 user=ana

def connect(host, port=5432, /, *, timeout=10):
    return f"{host}:{port} (timeout={timeout})"

print(connect("db", 6543, timeout=2))  # db:6543 (timeout=2)
# connect(host="db")       -> TypeError: positional-only
# connect("db", 1, 2)      -> TypeError: timeout is keyword-only

point = (3, 4)
opts = {"sep": " | ", "end": "!\n"}
print(*point, **opts)                  # 3 | 4!

def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):          # forward everything
    return connect(*args, **kwargs)
print(wrapper("api", timeout=1))       # api:5432 (timeout=1)
takeaways: `*args` is a tuple of extra positional arguments, `**kwargs` a dict of extra arguments passed by name
Parameters after `*` must be named; parameters before `/` can't be
`f(*seq, **mapping)` spreads values into a call
pitfalls: Hiding a function's real options behind `**kwargs`, so misspelled option names are silently ignored.

quiz.q: Given `def f(a, *, b): ...`, which call is valid?
quiz.explain: `b` comes after `*`, so it must be passed by name; `f(1, b=2)` is the only valid call.

quiz.q: What is `kwargs` inside `def g(**kwargs)` when called as `g(x=1, y=2)`?
quiz.explain: `**kwargs` gathers the extra keyword arguments into a dict.

concepts.name: Functions as objects, lambdas and closures
concepts.summary: Pass functions around like any value, write tiny lambda functions, and see how inner functions remember variables (closures).
concepts.why: Sorting by a key, reacting to events and decorators all rely on handing a function to other code.
concepts.body:
In Python a function is an object like any other. You can store it in a variable or a dict, pass it to another function, and return it from one. Languages that allow this are said to have **first-class functions**. `sorted(people, key=get_age)` passes the function `get_age` itself; note there are no brackets after it, because you're handing it over, not calling it.

A function you hand to other code for it to call later is often called a **callback**.

A **lambda** is a tiny function without a name, written in one expression: `lambda p: p["age"]` takes `p` and gives back `p["age"]`. It's ideal for short `key=` arguments. If you'd want to give it a name, or it grows beyond one simple expression, write a `def` instead. The `operator` module has ready-made ones such as `itemgetter("age")`.

Python looks up a name in a fixed order of places, called **scopes**: the current function first, then any function around it, then the module, then Python's built-ins. Inside a function you can define another function. The inner one can read the outer function's variables, and it keeps them alive even after the outer function has returned. A function together with the variables it remembers is a **closure**:

```python
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def increment():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return increment
```

Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local, so to change a remembered variable you declare it `nonlocal` (or `global` for a module-level one).

A classic surprise: closures remember **variables, not values**. Lambdas created in a loop all see the loop variable's last value. Fix it by copying the current value into a default argument (`lambda x=x: ...`), or use `functools.partial`, which makes a new function with some arguments already filled in.
concepts.code:
from functools import partial
from operator import itemgetter

people = [{"name": "Ana", "age": 31}, {"name": "Ben", "age": 27}]
print([p["name"] for p in sorted(people, key=lambda p: p["age"])])
# ['Ben', 'Ana']
print(max(people, key=itemgetter("age"))["name"])   # Ana

ops = {"add": lambda a, b: a + b, "mul": lambda a, b: a * b}
print(ops["mul"](6, 7))                # 42

def make_multiplier(factor):
    def multiply(x):
        return x * factor              # captures factor
    return multiply

print(make_multiplier(3)(5))           # 15
late = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in late])             # [2, 2, 2]
bound = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in bound])            # [0, 1, 2]

int_base2 = partial(int, base=2)
print(int_base2("1010"))               # 10
takeaways: Functions are values: pass them without brackets to hand them over
Use `lambda` only for short one-expression functions like sort keys
Closures remember variables, not values; use `nonlocal` to change them
pitfalls: Writing `key=get_age()` (calling it) instead of `key=get_age`.
Expecting lambdas made in a loop to remember each pass's value.

quiz.q: Given `funcs = [lambda: n for n in range(3)]`, what is `funcs[0]()`?
quiz.explain: Every lambda looks up `n` only when called, after the loop has finished with n == 2.

quiz.q: Inside a nested function, what does `nonlocal total` allow?
options: Changing the outer function's `total` from the inner function
quiz.explain: Without `nonlocal`, assigning to `total` would create a new local variable in the inner function.

concepts.name: Classes and instances
concepts.summary: Define your own kinds of object with class: __init__, self, methods, attributes and a useful __repr__.
concepts.why: Classes bundle data with the actions on it, and most packages you install hand you objects made from classes.
concepts.body:
Every value so far had a type Python provides: `str`, `list`, `dict`. A **class** lets you define your own type, such as `Account` or `Invoice`. The class is the blueprint; each object made from it is an **instance**. You create one by calling the class like a function: `Account("ana", 100)`. Creating an instance is called **instantiating** the class.

Values stored on an object are its **attributes**, read with a dot: `acct.owner`. The special method `__init__` sets up each new instance. Its first parameter, by convention called `self`, is the new object itself, so `self.owner = owner` stores an attribute on that one instance. Methods with double underscores on both sides, like `__init__`, are **special methods** (also called dunder methods, for "double underscore"): Python calls them for you at certain moments.

Functions written inside the class are its methods. `acct.deposit(50)` is shorthand for `Account.deposit(acct, 50)`: Python passes the instance as `self` automatically. That's all `self` is, an ordinary first parameter.

Variables assigned directly in the class body are **class attributes**, shared by every instance. They suit fixed values and defaults. Never put a list there and append to it per instance; all instances would share that one list. Create it in `__init__` instead.

Python has no way to make an attribute truly private. A leading underscore, `self._balance`, means "internal, don't touch from outside", and everyone respects it.

Give almost every class a `__repr__` method. It returns a string describing the object for programmers, shown in the REPL and in printed output. (`__str__` can add a friendlier version for `print()`.)

A line starting with `@` above a `def` is a **decorator**: it hands the function to other code that changes how it works. Two you'll see in classes are `@classmethod`, whose method receives the class (`cls`) instead of an instance, often used for extra ways to create objects like `from_string`; and `@staticmethod`, a plain function that just lives inside the class. The decorators lesson shows how they work.

If a class mostly holds data, a dataclass (a later lesson) writes `__init__` and `__repr__` for you.
takeaways: A class is a blueprint; calling it makes an instance, prepared by `__init__`
`self` is just the instance, passed automatically as the first argument
Set per-instance data in `__init__`; class-body variables are shared by all instances
pitfalls: Defining a class attribute like `items = []` and appending to it for each instance.

quiz.q: `acct.deposit(50)` is equivalent to which call?
quiz.explain: Calling a method on an instance passes that instance as `self` to the function defined in the class.

concepts.name: Inheritance, super() and composition
concepts.summary: Build a class on top of another with inheritance, reuse the parent's code with super(), and know when to combine objects instead.
concepts.why: Frameworks and Python's own error types are built on inheritance, and good design knows its limits.
concepts.body:
Often a new class is a more specific version of an existing one: a `Dog` is an `Animal`. `class Dog(Animal):` makes `Dog` a **subclass** of `Animal`, its **base class** (or parent). This is **inheritance**: `Dog` gets every attribute and method of `Animal` without retyping them. When you read `dog.name`, Python checks the instance, then `Dog`, then `Animal`.

A subclass can **override** any method by defining one with the same name; its version is used instead. To extend the parent's behaviour rather than replace it, call it through `super()`: `super().__init__(name)` runs the parent's `__init__` on this object.

A class can have more than one parent (`class C(A, B)`), called **multiple inheritance**. Python then searches the classes in a fixed order, the **method resolution order** (MRO); `C.__mro__` shows it. `super()` follows that order, so always use it rather than naming the parent class directly.

Multiple inheritance is mostly used for small **mixins**: classes that add one ability, like a `JsonMixin` providing `to_json()`. Keep them narrow and always call `super()`.

`isinstance(obj, Animal)` is true for instances of `Animal` and of every subclass; `issubclass(Dog, Animal)` checks classes. Every class ultimately inherits from `object`.

Sometimes a base class only describes what its subclasses must provide, without doing it itself: "every shape has an `area()`". Such a list of required methods is an **interface**, and a class that sets one but can't be used on its own is an **abstract class**. Inherit from `abc.ABC` and mark the required methods with `@abstractmethod`. Python then refuses to instantiate any class that hasn't defined them all.

Inheritance means "is a", and it ties the subclass closely to the parent's inner workings. When you just want to reuse what another class does, it's usually more flexible to hold an object of it in an attribute and call it: a `Car` has an `Engine`, it isn't one. This is called composition. Deep chains of inheritance are a warning sign in Python.
takeaways: Subclasses inherit and can override; `super()` calls the next class in the MRO
`abc.ABC` plus `@abstractmethod` define an interface subclasses must fill in
Prefer holding another object (has-a) when you only need to reuse its behaviour
pitfalls: Forgetting to call `super().__init__()` so parent attributes are never set.

quiz.q: Why prefer `super().__init__()` over `Parent.__init__(self)`?
options: It follows the MRO, so multiple inheritance works correctly
quiz.explain: `super()` hands over to the next class in the method resolution order, which keeps multiple-inheritance chains correct.

concepts.name: Exceptions in depth
concepts.summary: else and finally, your own families of exceptions, chaining errors with raise ... from, and exception groups.
concepts.why: Reliable code, and code other people build on, depends on raising and handling the right errors in the right way.
concepts.body:
A full `try` statement has four parts: `try`, one or more `except`, an optional `else` that runs only if no exception happened, and `finally`, which always runs, for clean-up. Putting follow-up code in `else` rather than in `try` keeps the guarded part small, so you don't accidentally catch errors from code you didn't mean to guard.

Exceptions are classes, arranged in a family tree whose root is `BaseException`. Errors in your program inherit from `Exception`. `KeyboardInterrupt` (pressing Ctrl-C) and `SystemExit` deliberately don't, so `except Exception:` won't block Ctrl-C. An `except` line also catches subclasses, so list them from most to least specific. Catch several kinds with a tuple: `except (KeyError, IndexError):`.

For a library or larger program, define your own family: one base class (`class PaymentError(Exception)`) and specific subclasses. Callers can then catch everything from you with one `except`, or just one particular case.

Inside an `except` block, a bare `raise` re-raises the current exception with its traceback intact. When you turn a low-level error into your own, link them with **chaining**: `raise ConfigError("bad config") from err`. The traceback then shows both, joined by "The above exception was the direct cause...". Use `from None` to hide the original when it's just noise.

Python 3.11 added `e.add_note("context")` to attach extra information. It also added **exception groups**: an `ExceptionGroup` bundles several unrelated errors, for example from several jobs running at the same time, and `except*` handles each matching kind within the group.
takeaways: `else` runs when no exception happened; `finally` always runs
Make your own errors subclasses of one base class that inherits from `Exception`
Use `raise New(...) from err` to link errors, and bare `raise` to re-raise
pitfalls: Putting `except Exception:` before more specific `except` lines, so those never run.

quiz.q: When does the `else` block of a try statement run?
options: Only if the `try` block raised no exception
Only if an exception was caught
quiz.explain: `else` runs after `try` completes without raising, and before `finally`.

quiz.q: Which exception is NOT caught by `except Exception:`?
quiz.explain: KeyboardInterrupt inherits from BaseException directly, so Ctrl-C still stops the program.

concepts.name: Dataclasses
concepts.summary: Let @dataclass write __init__, __repr__ and == for classes that mainly hold data.
concepts.why: Most classes you write hold data; dataclasses remove the repetitive code and the bugs that hide in it.
concepts.body:
Many classes just hold a few values: an `Order` with an id, items and a total. Writing `__init__`, `__repr__` and an equality check by hand for each is repetitive, and code you have to repeat like this is called **boilerplate**. The `@dataclass` decorator writes it for you.

You list the class's **fields** (its data attributes) with type hints, `id: int`, and `@dataclass` generates `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` (which makes `==` compare field by field). Fields without defaults must come before fields with defaults, just as in a function's parameters.

Defaults that can change need care. `tags: list[str] = []` is rejected with a `ValueError`, because one list would be shared by every instance. Write `field(default_factory=list)` to get a fresh list per instance.

Useful options on the decorator:

- `frozen=True` makes instances immutable (assigning a field raises an error), so they can be dict keys or set items
- `order=True` adds `<`, `<=` and so on, comparing fields in order like a tuple
- `slots=True` makes each instance use less memory
- `kw_only=True` makes every field keyword-only

Put checks or calculated fields in a method called `__post_init__`; the generated `__init__` calls it at the end. `dataclasses.asdict(obj)` converts an instance to a dict, and `dataclasses.replace(obj, field=new)` makes a changed copy, which is how you "change" a frozen instance.

The type hints are needed to declare a field but are **not checked** while running: `Point("a", "b")` is accepted. To check and convert data that comes from outside, such as JSON sent by another program, libraries like Pydantic build on the same idea.

Compared with a named tuple (see the collections lesson), a dataclass can be changed by default, can't be indexed like a tuple, and is easier to extend with methods.
takeaways: `@dataclass` writes `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` from the fields' type hints
Use `field(default_factory=list)` for list or dict defaults
`frozen=True` gives unchangeable values; `replace()` makes changed copies
pitfalls: Assuming the type hints on fields are checked while the program runs.

quiz.q: Why does `@dataclass class C: xs: list = []` fail?
options: A shared mutable default is rejected; use default_factory
quiz.explain: A plain list default would be shared by all instances, so dataclasses raise ValueError and point you to default_factory.

concepts.name: Iterators and generators
concepts.summary: How for loops really work underneath, and how to write lazy sequences with yield.
concepts.why: Generators handle huge or endless data using little memory, and much of the standard library is built on them.
concepts.body:
A `for` loop asks its iterable for an **iterator**: an object that hands out items one at a time and remembers where it is, like a bookmark. Each time the loop needs the next item it calls `next()` on the iterator; when there's nothing left, the iterator raises `StopIteration` and the loop ends. You can do this by hand with the built-ins `iter()` and `next()`.

A list is iterable but isn't itself an iterator, so you can loop over it as often as you like; each loop gets a fresh iterator. Some objects, such as an open file or a generator, are their own iterator, so they can be gone through only **once**.

A **generator** function is any function containing `yield`. Calling it doesn't run the body; it gives back a generator object. Each `next()` runs the body until the next `yield`, which hands out a value and pauses there, keeping all its local variables. When the function ends, the iteration ends.

Generators are lazy: they work out a value only when asked. That lets you:

- process files far larger than memory, one line or item at a time
- describe endless sequences (`itertools.count()` counts forever) and take only what you need
- build a **pipeline**: a chain of steps where each generator takes its input from the one before

A generator expression `(f(x) for x in xs)` is the one-line form.

The `itertools` module is a toolbox for iterators: `islice` (take a slice of any iterator), `chain`, `groupby`, `accumulate`, `pairwise` and `batched`. Built-ins such as `zip`, `map`, `filter`, `enumerate` and `reversed` also give back lazy iterators.
